title: Quarto Manual
text:
0.1 Introduction
{{ << include README.md >> }}
A Quarto Manual is a structured, multi-document Quarto template. It contains ordered, executable .qmd pages, workflow-specific helper libraries, page-level tests, and a final readiness checklist. Organizations, research groups, and individuals can create their own Quarto Manuals to document and share procedural, complex workflows.
Manuals are common in many workplaces and every day life:
When instructions are more complex than simply reading can allow, manuals are employed to ensure that critical procedures are followed correctly and consistently, and — perhaps most importantly — rely on active participation from the user and frequent spot checks to ensure that the workflow is going smoothly.
Working with software need not be any different.

Quarto Manuals are interactive, executable software manuals for setting up and operating research computing projects. They are designed to be used by researchers, students, and other users who need to follow complex workflows in a consistent and reproducible manner.

Quarto Manual
text:
0.3 Creating a new manual
To create a manual for your own workflow, start with a Quarto project and use the quarto-manual project type or extension in _quarto.yml:
project:
  type: quarto-manual
Then create one .qmd page for each setup step in your workflow.
Each page should contain:

a short explanation of what the step does;
a code chunk that discovers the current project state;
any user-editable variables for that step;
code or export blocks that create the required files;
an inspection or test that proves the step is complete.

For example:
# 02 Request Specification

## Start from current project state

```python
from quarto_manual.project import Project

project = Project.discover()
```

## Assemble

Create the request specification for this project.

## Inspect

Run the page-level check that confirms the request specification exists and is valid.

1.1 How to run this demonstration
Render normally to see the callouts:
quarto render template.qmd
Run with export enabled to write the generated files:
RSE_MANUAL_EXPORT=1 quarto render template.qmd
Run in check mode to see what would be written without changing files:
RSE_MANUAL_EXPORT=1 RSE_MANUAL_CHECK=1 quarto render template.qmd
Override metadata variables with environment variables:
RSE_MANUAL_EXPORT=1 \
RSE_MANUAL_VAR_PROJECT_NAME="my-era5-project" \
RSE_MANUAL_VAR_PROJECT_PACKAGE="my_era5_project" \
RSE_MANUAL_VAR_PROJECT_DIR="generated/my-era5-project" \
RSE_MANUAL_VAR_PACKAGE_ROOT="generated/my-era5-project/src/my_era5_project" \
quarto render template.qmd

text:
1.4 1. Manual library export

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path
import subprocess


def expect_file(path: str | Path) -> Path:
    """Assert that a file exists and return it as a Path."""
    path = Path(path)
    assert path.exists(), f"Expected path to exist: {path}"
    assert path.is_file(), f"Expected file: {path}"
    return path


def expect_dir(path: str | Path) -> Path:
    """Assert that a directory exists and return it as a Path."""
    path = Path(path)
    assert path.exists(), f"Expected path to exist: {path}"
    assert path.is_dir(), f"Expected directory: {path}"
    return path


def expect_command_succeeds(command: list[str]) -> None:
    """Assert that a command exits successfully."""
    result = subprocess.run(
        command,
        check=False,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
    )

    assert result.returncode == 0, (
        "Command failed: "
        + " ".join(command)
        + "\nSTDOUT:\n"
        + result.stdout
        + "\nSTDERR:\n"
        + result.stderr
    )

This block demonstrates .manual-lib-source.
When exported, it writes a reusable manual-library helper module to:
{{ manual_root }}/src/quarto_manual/checks.py
Because the code block language is python, the export filter adds a # comment header.

text:
1.7 4. Project script export

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

project_dir="{{ project_dir }}"

echo "Checking project directory: ${project_dir}"

test -d "${project_dir}"
test -d "${project_dir}/config"
test -d "${project_dir}/src" || mkdir -p "${project_dir}/src"
test -d "${project_dir}/tests" || mkdir -p "${project_dir}/tests"

echo "Project scaffold exists."

This block demonstrates .manual-project-script.
The mode="0755" attribute demonstrates executable script export. When the filter writes the file, it should call chmod 0755 for this target.
When exported, it writes:
{{ project_dir }}/scripts/check_project.sh

title: Quarto Manual
text:
1.8 5. Project test export

from pathlib import Path

from {{ project_package }}.contract import ProjectContract


def test_project_contract_discovers_project():
    project = ProjectContract.discover()

    assert project.project_name == "{{ project_name }}"
    assert project.project_package == "{{ project_package }}"
    assert project.project_dir.name == Path("{{ project_dir }}").name


def test_project_contract_paths_are_named():
    project = ProjectContract.discover()

    assert project.src_dir.name == "src"
    assert project.tests_dir.name == "tests"
    assert project.config_dir.name == "config"

This block demonstrates .manual-project-test.
When exported, it writes:
{{ project_dir }}/tests/test_project_contract.py
This is the page-level inspection artifact. It asks whether the project contract generated by this page is usable.

text:
1.14 11. Notes for manual authors
Each export block should obey these rules:

Include exactly one export class.
Include a file="..." attribute.
Contain exactly one code block.
Use template variables only when they are declared in YAML metadata or passed through environment variables.
Keep explanatory prose outside export blocks unless the prose itself is the exported artifact.
Use .manual-run for code that should run in the page but should not be exported.
Use .manual-explain for conceptual explanation that should render as a callout but should not be exported.

This page intentionally demonstrates the full contract expected by the current filters.

title: 2  Quarto Manuals
text:
2.1 Checklist Structure
A Quarto Manual is an executable operations manual for a project. It helps the user assemble, configure, inspect, and verify the project so that the work can be done deliberately and visibly.
One useful way to think about a manual is through aviation. One pilot’s flight manual might cover route preparation, security and safety checks, pre-flight routines, operation, inspection, and periodic verification of the aircraft integrity during flight, takeoff and landing procedures, and emergency protocols. In the same way, a Quarto Manual can break up cognitively complex software workflows into manageable steps for yourself and your users.
It can guide setup and installation, operating procedures, and checks across the life of a project.
Checklists and pages can be useful abstractions for describing a manual:
In addition, pages can have semantic meaning that gives us operational structure:
A well-designed manual should move in order from page to page. Earlier pages establish conditions that later pages rely on. By the time the user reaches the final page, they should be able to answer questions like:
A Quarto Manual checklist is derived from the manual’s ordered pages. Each page should have a clear purpose and should leave behind evidence that the step was completed. That evidence should usually come from the real project state: files, directories, configuration, rendered outputs, logs, and passing checks.
We’ll use the page metadata to declare where a page belongs in the checklist:
The manual.page field gives the page its place in the manual. The checklist view can then use that ordering to summarize the manual, report missing sections, and help the user see how much of the procedure has been covered.

3  Manual Python Implementation
text:
3.1 Implementation
Python is great for object oriented workflows. One useful Python implementation for a manual is as a Checklist object. By using a dataclass, we can create a flexible checklist object that summarize a manual and its pages. In that design, the checklist is not the manual itself. It is a structured representation of the manual’s ordered steps. Each page has a number, title, and semantic content for prerequisite, procedure, and check blocks.

5.1 Required Page Structure
Each Quarto Manual page is one operational step in the manual. A page should tell the user:
To make that structure explicit, every page must use three semantic block types:
These blocks give the page a predictable structure for both the reader and the manual tooling. They also let the manual derive a checklist view across all pages without turning the manual into a hidden workflow engine.

5.1.1 1. Prerequisite Block
The prerequisite block explains what the user must already have before this step is actionable. This is the place to inspect the current project state, load shared helper code, or confirm that earlier manual steps are complete.
There must be exactly one prerequisite block on the page. In this manual, the prerequisite block should include the shared checklist definition so that each page starts from the same declared manual state.1
